### Steering makes tokens compete {#steering-makes-tokens-compete} {{< panel "info" >}} **The short version.** Steering changes both factors of the loop's derivative: the readout, by moving which tokens compete, and the network's Jacobian. Three measurements on Qwen2.5-0.5B say that, along the orbits we recorded, the growth that steering adds comes mainly from the readout, where next tokens compete. In chaotic cells the readout stretches differences by 2.58 nats per step more than in nearly unsteered cells, while the network factor barely changes; a bias on the logits alone, with the network unsteered, makes part of the plane chaotic; and along recorded orbits, swapping in the steered readout alone raises the growth, while swapping in the steered network alone damps it. These are comparisons along recorded orbits, not a proof that the readout change alone sustains the chaos. {{< /panel >}} Steering could create chaos through either factor of the derivative: it moves the logits, and with them which tokens compete in \(\Sigma_p\), and it moves the hidden states, and with them the network's response \(J_{\tilde h}\). Three measurements on Qwen2.5-0.5B, steered along the philosophy direction, tell the two apart (Figure 13; details in Figure 12 and Table 2). **A gain split.** Recall the chain of one step. The state \(x\), the vector fed back as the input at the soft-token position, goes through the steered transformer to its final normalized hidden state \(\tilde h\) at that position; from \(\tilde h\), the logits and the softmax lead to the next state \(F(x)\), the probability-weighted average of the token embeddings. A small change \(\delta x\) of the state therefore causes a change \(\delta\tilde h\) of the hidden state and a change \(\delta F\) of the next state, and each step's relative growth splits exactly into a network factor and a readout factor, \[ g_{\mathrm{net}} = \frac{\lvert\delta\tilde h\rvert/\lvert\tilde h\rvert}{\lvert\delta x\rvert/\lvert x\rvert}, \qquad g_{\mathrm{read}} = \frac{\lvert\delta F\rvert/\lvert F\rvert}{\lvert\delta\tilde h\rvert/\lvert\tilde h\rvert}, \] the relative stretch through the network and the relative stretch through the readout. Follow a small difference for \(n\) steps along an orbit \(x_0, \dots, x_n\): the average logarithms of the two factors add up to its growth rate over those steps plus a boundary term, \((\log\lVert x_0\rVert - \log\lVert x_n\rVert)/n\), which appears because every change is measured relative to the size of the state, and which shrinks as \(n\) grows. Both factors are relative gains along the orbit, not the largest stretch the matrices can apply (their operator norms). The split depends on how the intermediate state is measured, so only the sum is intrinsic, and the comparisons are between cells within one convention. Over a 101 × 53 scan in steering strength and temperature (layer 12; 5353 cells, 331 chaotic), the chaotic cells' readout factor exceeds that of nearly unsteered cells (\(\lvert\alpha\rvert \le 0.01\)) at the same temperature by 2.58 nats per step (95% interval [1.78, 3.59] over 18 temperature rows; 321 chaotic and 162 nearly unsteered cells). Their network factor differs by only \(-0.07\) [−0.23, 0.12]. With nearly no steering the readout's relative gain shrinks differences strongly, by 0.87 to 5.49 nats per step. In the chaotic cells it grows them, except in the three highest temperature rows (\(\log_{10}T = 0.175\) to 0.225), where it still shrinks them, but less. Compared with periodic cells at the same temperature, chaotic cells have a higher next-token entropy (+1.62 nats, [1.26, 1.91]), a smaller gap between the two largest logits (−1.37 in units of \(T\), [−1.98, −0.87]) and a larger readout factor (+1.36, [0.91, 1.93]), each with \(p \le 10^{-4}\) in a permutation test within temperature rows (see {{< refterm "p-value" "p-value" >}}). **A test that leaves the network unsteered.** We add to the logits a bias \(\beta\,b\) along \(Wv\), the output matrix applied to the steering vector, a stand-in in logit space for the steering (for Qwen2.5-0.5B the output matrix is the embedding matrix \(E\); \(b\) is centered and scaled to unit standard deviation over the vocabulary), with no residual steering. At any given state this changes only the output probabilities, although the orbit it produces can visit different states. On its grid, 3.5% of cells were chaotic (241 of 6837, all but one with a nonzero bias), against 6.2% on the residual-steering grid (331 of 5353). The two grids share their temperature rows but not a matched strength of intervention, so these are counts per grid, not a comparison of doses. A change of the output probabilities alone, with the network unsteered, therefore suffices for chaotic cells in part of the plane, mostly at \(\log_{10}T \ge 0.1\) (207 of the 241 cells), where the network factor itself can expand; below that temperature, 34 of the 5676 cells of the bias grid are chaotic (0.6%), against 169 of 4444 (3.8%) under residual steering. **An orbit-preserving crossover.** A gain split compares different orbits, so steering could act simply by moving the orbit to other states. A crossover at fixed states separates the two contributions. Along recorded steered orbits we evaluated the steered and the unsteered model at the same states and carried four tangent dynamics, each pairing the steered or unsteered readout with the steered or unsteered network Jacobian (call them 11, 10, 01 and 00, readout first). A validation fixed in advance, that the fully steered version 11 reproduce the twin exponent within 0.02 at every cell, holds at 23 of 24 cells, all within 0.012; at the remaining periodic cell, which contracts at about \(-12\) per step, the twin offset falls to the rounding floor. A sufficiency criterion fixed in advance, that version 10 come within 0.1 of version 11 on average, fails by overshoot: steering only the readout gives more growth than the full steered map, by 0.23, because steering's change of the network damps it. Versions 10 and 01 are hybrids: tangent products assembled step by step along the recorded states, each step pairing one model's readout with the other model's network Jacobian. They are not the dynamics of a hybrid model run anew from those states, but a bookkeeping device that apportions the growth along the recorded orbits. Over 14 chaotic cells reserved for this test, steering only the readout (version 10 against 00) raises the finite-time growth by 0.81 nats per step ([0.29, 1.35]); steering only the network response (01 against 00) lowers it by 0.49 ([−0.63, −0.35]); the interaction is +0.26 ([0.09, 0.45]). Below \(\log_{10}T = 0\) the steered readout turns the contraction of the unsteered derivative (−1.03 nats per step) into growth (+0.72), more than the full steered map shows (+0.34). Above it, the unsteered derivative already expands at the steered states (+0.41), and steering may act by bringing the orbit there. In Qwen2.5-7B, whose embeddings are untied, the same crossover (18 cells of its steered map at layer 14; version 11 equals the twin exponent within \(10^{-4}\) at every cell) reproduces the damping: over its 10 reserved chaotic cells, steering only the network response lowers the growth by 1.14 nats per step ([−1.61, −0.64]), and steering only the readout adds +0.23 ([−0.11, 0.63], an interval that includes zero). ### Unsteered chaos and steering controls {#controls} {{< panel "info" >}} **The short version.** Steering is a probe, not the cause. Without any steering, temperature alone makes the loop chaotic in most dense models we swept. Steering widens the chaotic regions, but random directions of the same size do so about as often as concept directions; what a direction selects is the text of the attractors. {{< /panel >}} Steering adds a fixed vector to the residual stream, so chaos along a steering axis could belong to the push rather than to the model. At \(\alpha = 0\), however, the map is the unsteered model's own feedback map, with temperature as its only parameter. The \(\alpha = 0\) columns of the hostility maps contain cells with positive finite-horizon exponents in Llama-3.1-8B (26 of 64 temperatures), Qwen2.5-7B (15 of 64) and OLMo-2-7B (11 of 64), while the near-zero columns of the 0.5B and 1.5B maps contain one such cell each (of 128 and 64). Across the prompts we tested, the prompt decides where the chaos lies, not whether it occurs. ### What theory allows, and how many dimensions the chaos has {#theory-context} **What theory allows.** Chaos and periodic windows occur in many nonlinear feedback systems. In a specified ensemble of random recurrent networks with asymmetric couplings, chaos sets in above a critical gain, sharply in the large-network limit, and finite networks pass through limit cycles of increasing complexity on the way ([Sompolinsky, Crisanti, and Sommers, 1988](#ref-sompolinsky-1988)); how the transition looks depends on the architecture and the transfer function ([Kadmon and Sompolinsky, 2015](#ref-kadmon-2015)). Discrete-time random networks, \(x(t+1) = \tanh(gJx(t))\), iterate a map as our loop does: their fixed point loses stability when the gain times the spectral radius of the couplings exceeds one, the first bifurcation of large networks is a Neimark-Sacker bifurcation, in which a complex pair of multipliers crosses the unit circle and a closed invariant curve is born ([Kuznetsov, 2023](#ref-kuznetsov-2023)), and chaos follows by a quasi-periodic route, through a torus and frequency locking, over a range of gain that narrows as the network grows ([Doyon et al., 1994](#ref-doyon-1994)). Our largest model narrows differently: Qwen2.5-72B passes from a confident echo to a nearly uniform fixed point within 0.03 decades of temperature, and its chaos is confined to narrow bands, whereas in random networks chaos is generic above the transition. External input can suppress that chaos ([Rajan, Abbott, and Sompolinsky, 2010](#ref-rajan-2010)), and deep networks at initialization show an order-to-chaos transition in signal propagation ([Poole et al., 2016](#ref-poole-2016); [Schoenholz et al., 2017](#ref-schoenholz-2017)). In our map, temperature plays the role of an inverse gain and the steering vector that of an input. The factorization of the derivative makes the correspondence concrete, with the softmax derivative \((\mathrm{diag}\,p - pp^{\top})/T\) in the place of the slope of the transfer function; the identification with the random-network transition remains an analogy, not a transfer of that ensemble's theorem. Periodic windows, shrimp-shaped domains with their cusps and spirals, and doubling cascades are found in many dissipative two-parameter systems ([Gallas, 1993](#ref-gallas-1993); [Bonatto and Gallas, 2008](#ref-bonatto-2008); [Vitolo, Glendinning, and Gallas, 2011](#ref-vitolo-2011); [Façanha, Oldeman, and Glass, 2013](#ref-facanha-2013)) and in experiments ([Stoop, Benner, and Uwate, 2010](#ref-stoop-2010)). **Contraction and expansion in the network.** Analyses of deep attention identify contracting tendencies: pure self-attention collapses token representations toward a common vector with depth ([Dong, Cordonnier, and Loukas, 2021](#ref-dong-2021)), and idealized attention dynamics form clusters ([Geshkovski et al., 2023](#ref-geshkovski-2023)). Residual connections and MLPs counteract the collapse. Which tendency wins along an orbit is a property of the trained weights that only computation settles. In every dense model we mapped, both outcomes occur: the same map has negative largest exponents in some regions of its parameter plane and positive ones in others. **The dimension of the chaos.** Near a periodic orbit, the multipliers measure how many directions the dynamics keeps. For chaotic attractors the corresponding measure is the Kaplan-Yorke dimension ([Kaplan and Yorke, 1979](#ref-kaplan-1979)), \[ D_{\mathrm{KY}} = j + \frac{\sum_{i\le j}\lambda_i}{\lvert\lambda_{j+1}\rvert}, \] with \(j\) the largest index at which the partial sum of the ordered Lyapunov exponents is still nonnegative; with one positive exponent and \(\lambda_1 + \lambda_2 < 0\), \(D_{\mathrm{KY}} = 1 + \lambda_1/\lvert\lambda_2\rvert\). Read it as the number of directions in which the attractor spreads: 1 for chaos that lives on a curve, between 1 and 2 for a thin, layered sheet. We estimated the four leading exponents by QR iteration (1000 transient and 2000 measured steps, float64) at 35 completed cells: 28 chosen by percentile of their largest exponent before any of their spectra were seen (of 30 requested), and seven from the earlier horizon check, six chaotic and one periodic control. At this horizon 31 have a positive leading estimate and none has two positive estimates. These are finite-time estimates, not asymptotic dimensions, and they grow with temperature. - Along the hostile temperature line, where a scalar return relation fits ([Chaos behind a repeating text](#chaos-behind-a-repeating-text)), eight chaotic cells have \(D_{\mathrm{KY}} = 1.008\) to 1.16, consistent with nearly one-dimensional chaos. - At fourteen chaotic cells of the headline maps (\(\log_{10}T\) from \(-0.17\) to \(-0.04\)) it is 1.03 to 1.65, rising with \(\lambda_1\). - In the high-temperature region (\(\log_{10}T\) from \(-0.02\) to 0.13), nine chaotic cells have \(D_{\mathrm{KY}} = 1.37\) to 2.02; at two of them the sum of the first two estimates is nonnegative: over this horizon, small areas spanned by two directions do not shrink, although only one estimated exponent is positive (a nonnegative sum is not a second expanding direction). A scalar return map therefore describes the low-temperature chaos well and the high-temperature chaos poorly, consistent with the large second multipliers of the high-temperature bubble. The number of competing tokens does not set the dimension. The readout's trace-to-leading-eigenvalue ratio, \(\mathrm{tr}\,\Sigma_p/\lambda_{\max}(\Sigma_p)\) averaged along the orbit, counts the directions in which the readout amplifies comparably. \(D_{\mathrm{KY}}\) never exceeds it and rises with it within each group of cells (Spearman 0.72 over 17 philosophy cells and 0.69 over 8 hostile cells, computed when the data came in and not independently reproduced; both are confounded with temperature). Across groups it does not predict the dimension: the hostile cells have ratios of about 16 to 19 and next-token entropies of about 7 to 9 nats, yet \(D_{\mathrm{KY}} \le 1.16\) (Figure 12f). The readout supplies many competing directions; the network decides how many of them expand. ### Stretch, squeeze and fold in the loop {#stretch-squeeze-fold} {{< panel "info" >}} **The short version.** The competition between next tokens stretches: a small change of the state shifts probability between two of them and moves the next soft token by more than the change. The network and the succession of steps squeeze every other direction: in the directions we measured, small differences shrink strongly, which is why a description by one number is worth trying in a space of 896 dimensions. The network also folds: its response bends the stretched set back over itself, so that, read through a single coordinate, two different states lead to the same next value. One-humped return maps, fitted on the sampled range, and doubling ratios that approach Feigenbaum's constant are consistent with that fold; they motivate a one-dimensional description, although no global one-dimensional reduction is established. {{< /panel >}} **What stretches: the competition between continuations.** When two next tokens with different embeddings share the probability, a small change of the state shifts weight from one to the other, and the next soft token moves along the line between their embeddings by more than the change: the readout gain \(\Sigma_p/T\) exceeds 1 along that line, as in case (c) of [the two-token cases](#two-token-gain-cases). In the chaotic cells at low temperature the gain split puts the stretching there: the readout factor grows differences by a median of 0.46 to 0.74 nats per step, while the network factor shrinks them ([Steering makes tokens compete](#steering-makes-tokens-compete)). The split is a bookkeeping convention along recorded orbits, so this says where the stretch shows up, not what ultimately causes it. At higher temperature the network can carry the stretch instead. Stretching within one step is common and decides nothing: nearly every step stretches some direction, in periodic cells as much as in chaotic ones ([Stability belongs to the loop](#stability-belongs-to-the-loop)). What marks a chaotic cell is that the stretching survives the whole orbit, so that its largest Lyapunov exponent is positive, with medians of 0.30 and 0.17 nats per step in the chaotic cells of the two main maps. **What squeezes: the network and the succession of steps.** The readout passes on only the directions in which the probable tokens' embeddings differ, and with many competing tokens that still leaves several: along the orbits, the second eigenvalue of \(\Sigma_p\) is 0.23 to 0.87 of the first. The decisive squeeze happens over several steps. Successive steps stretch different directions, their stretches do not line up, and most of each step's stretch is undone by the steps that follow, so that over a cycle one direction dominates far more than in any single step. Over twelve steps of the chaotic crescent, the second singular value of the composed map is \(3\times10^{-4}\) of the first, and in the chaotic stripes \(4\times10^{-9}\). At three chaotic cells, one in the crescent's chaotic core and two among the chaotic stripes, the next three Lyapunov exponents lie between \(-0.82\) and \(-2.01\) per step, against leading exponents of 0.109 to 0.424 ([Evidence for low-dimensional dynamics](#why-one-dimension)). The Kaplan-Yorke dimension is 1.03 to 1.65 at fourteen chaotic cells of the main maps and reaches about 2 only in the high-temperature region ([the dimension of the chaos](#theory-context)). These finite spectra show strong contraction in the directions we sampled, which is why a picture with one or two dimensions is worth trying; they do not show that the attractor lies on a curve. This is the ingredient the toy loop cannot show: it has a single direction, so it can only stretch and fold. The real loop has 895 more, and squeezing them is what motivates a one-dimensional picture of it, although no global one-dimensional reduction is established. **What folds: the network's response.** The stretching cannot go on forever, because the soft token never leaves the {{< refterm "convex-hull" "convex hull" >}} of the embeddings and no probability exceeds 1. Something must bend the stretched set back, and in a tied-embedding model the readout cannot do it alone. Without the network the loop lowers an energy at every step: it can stretch, but it never turns back, and it has neither cycles nor chaos ([Why the network-free map cannot cycle](#network-free-map)). Toy model A shows the same in one dimension: its curve without a network stretches in the middle, yet the orbit settles. The fold comes from the network. In the toy it is a logit gap that first rises and then falls as the soft token moves toward one token. In the language model it shows in the return maps of chaotic cells, which plot where the state lands one cycle later against where it was. Next to the hostile period-7 body, at coarse resolution, they have a single hump (Figures 37 and 38): in the plotted coordinate two different values lead to the same next value, so that coordinate cannot tell which of them the loop came from. A one-dimensional map fitted to such a hump, on the sampled range, closely reproduces the full map's exponent in most cells of the hostile cascade (Figure 40). The period-doubling cascades give independent, finite evidence consistent with the fold. The intervals between successive doublings shrink by ratios that approach Feigenbaum's constant, the last one to within 0.008%. Such scaling holds within a universality class: suitable families of maps whose single smooth hump has a quadratic top, including suitable strongly dissipative families of higher dimension (a hump with a flatter top has a different constant). The ratios alone do not establish that the loop reduces to such a map ([Feigenbaum ratios](#feigenbaum-ratios)). A horseshoe, the object that a strict proof of chaos would exhibit, is these three operations made exact: two thin regions of states that a few steps stretch across both, squeeze in every other direction and fold back onto themselves ([the open challenge](#numerics-and-chaos-labels)). ## What the chaos does to reproducibility {#reproducibility} Language-model inference is not bitwise reproducible: GPU kernels choose different reduction orders for different matrix shapes, so a request's result depends on its batch layout, the set of requests that the GPU processes together with it, and on the hardware ([He and Thinking Machines Lab, 2025](#ref-he-2025); [Yuan et al., 2025](#ref-yuan-2025)). In a chaotic loop, such rounding differences are not harmless. This section explains how a change of batch reaches the output, measures it, and draws the practical consequence. It ends with seven further tests, exploratory unless stated: whether the same sensitivity lets a deliberate perturbation steer an answer, whether the sensitivity can be tamed or used, whether weight quantization moves the attractors, whether a prompt's chaos onset predicts where sampled text stops repeating, a behavioral check of two coupled agents, whether the history of a steering schedule changes a decision (with a confirmatory rerun), and whether hidden differences behind an identical text change the answers to follow-up questions. ### How a change of batch reaches the output {#batch-to-output} Two runs of the same request can differ on the same machine for a reason that has nothing to do with sampling. Floating-point addition is not associative: every addition rounds its result to a representable number, so \((a+b)+c\) and \(a+(b+c)\) can differ in the last bit ([Goldberg, 1991](#ref-goldberg-1991)). A matrix multiplication in a transformer sums thousands of products, and GPU libraries split and order those sums according to the shape of the matrices, to keep the hardware busy. The number of requests processed together, the batch, is part of that shape. The same request computed alone or in a batch therefore receives results that differ at the rounding level: about \(10^{-16}\) relative in float64 and about \(10^{-3}\) in bfloat16. In a single forward pass such differences are invisible. In a feedback loop they are not lost. Each output becomes the next input, so the difference \(\delta_t\) between the two runs is fed back and transformed by the map's derivative at every step. To first order, and apart from the new rounding difference that each step adds, \[ \delta_{t+1} \approx DF(x_t)\,\delta_t . \] On a periodic attractor the derivative contracts on average and the Lyapunov exponent is negative: the difference decays until both runs follow the same orbit and write the same text. On a chaotic attractor the exponent \(\lambda\) is positive, and the difference grows like \(d_1 e^{\lambda t}\) from its first value \(d_1\). It therefore reaches a relative size of \(10^{-2}\) after about \[ t_* \approx \frac{\ln(10^{-2}/d_1)}{\lambda} \] steps (about 100 steps for \(d_1 \approx 10^{-15}\) and \(\lambda \approx 0.3\)). At most a few Lyapunov times (of \(1/\lambda\) steps each) later, at 1.27 to 176% of the state's norm in the examples of [Table 1](#what-a-chaotic-loop-writes) (0 to 16 steps after the distance passes \(10^{-2}\)), the two runs write different text. Because \(t_*\) depends on the starting difference only through its logarithm, finer rounding delays the divergence of a chaotic loop but does not prevent it. ### What batch-invariant kernels can and cannot fix {#batch-invariant-kernels} The practical consequence follows from the same picture. Batch-invariant kernels, which fix the order of every reduction independently of the batch size, remove this source of difference ([He and Thinking Machines Lab, 2025](#ref-he-2025)). In a periodic regime that is enough, and small differences would be forgiven even without it. In a chaotic regime it is not: other small differences, from another GPU model, a library or compiler version, a mathematically equivalent reordering of a sum, or float32 arithmetic in place of float64, generically grow at the same rate, so a run is reproducible only if the whole computation is repeated bit for bit. The measurements cover the last of these directly: float32 and float64 runs of the same chaotic cells also separate (all 192 pass \(10^{-2}\), after a median of 20 steps). Numerical differences are the disturbance; the feedback dynamics decide whether it grows. How far it grows within a given budget also depends on its starting size, on the horizon and on how close the run comes to a change of answer, so a periodic loop can still change an answer when the starting difference is large. ### A control with the shapes held fixed {#fixed-shape-control} If this account is right, two predictions follow, and a test fixed in advance checked both on the same 448 cells. First, if the matrix shapes do not change, nothing should differ at all. That held exactly. With the shapes fixed, the two runs are bitwise identical over all 1500 steps in every cell, both when the same rows run twice and when the rows are permuted, so that every cell has other neighbors and another position in the batch. No information passes between rows; the only route for a difference is the order of the sums, which the shape decides. Second, a difference put in by hand should grow like the batch difference does. With the shapes fixed, each cell's start was displaced by a relative amount \(d\), from \(10^{-15}\), the size of the rounding difference, up to \(10^{-3}\). In the chaotic cells the displacement passes \(10^{-2}\) after about \(\ln(10^{-2}/d)/\lambda\) steps, the number the exponent predicts. For \(d\) from \(10^{-15}\) to \(10^{-7}\) the median ratio of measured to predicted steps is 0.87, 1.01, 1.08, 1.10 and 1.18. Only for the largest displacements, which are no longer small, does the linear account fail. In the periodic cells a tiny displacement dies out. Larger ones sometimes separate the runs, in up to 59% of cells at \(d = 10^{-3}\), presumably by pushing the state across a basin boundary into another attractor's basin (the attractors the displaced runs reached were not classified). ### The same problems, a different batch {#answers} Low precision changes the starting point. In bfloat16 the starting difference is already about \(10^{-3}\), so continuous feedback can carry it into different answers within a short budget even where the float64 loop is not chaotic. A test at the level of answers, designed before the runs, measured this. We asked Qwen2.5-0.5B 96 two-digit additions, not used before, through a short soft-thinking pipeline: for 32 steps the model is fed the probability-weighted average of its token embeddings, each new one appended to a growing context, and a fixed answer cue then reads the number off greedily. Each problem ran alone and in a batch with three fixed distractor problems of the same length. Nothing is padded, so the two runs compute the same quantities and differ only in how the GPU groups its sums, that is, by rounding. In bfloat16 the extracted answer changed with the batch layout in 56% of the problems at \(T = 1\) and in 8% at \(T = 10^{0.2}\). At \(T = 1\) the pipeline answers 23 of the 96 problems correctly alone and 22 in the batch, so most changes are between wrong answers; at \(T = 10^{0.4}\), where it answers 90 of the 96 correctly in both layouts, no answer changed. A forced greedy baseline with the same budget (32 greedy tokens, then the same cue) produced identical token sequences in both layouts for every problem. The excess disagreement of soft over greedy decoding, averaged over the two temperatures, is 32.3 percentage points (95% interval [26.5, 38.1]). (The forced greedy baseline's accuracy is zero and not informative: forced through 32 tokens, the model writes past its answer, and the cue then extracts another number.) The same test in Qwen2.5-7B, whose soft-thinking pipeline answers 51 to 64% of these problems at \(T = 10^{0.2}\), replicates the result. In bfloat16 the batch layout changed the soft-thinking answer in 53 of the 96 problems (55%) at \(T = 10^{0.2}\), the temperature at which the soft trace still matters. In 24 of these 53 problems one layout gave no number (an invalid answer, which the design fixed in advance counts as a value); in the other 29 (30% of the problems) both gave numbers, and they differ. The pipeline answered 49 of the 96 correctly alone and 61 in the batch; at \(T = 10^{0.4}\) it answered all 96 correctly in both layouts, and no answer changed. At this precision even the forced greedy baseline changed in 10 of the 96, the known batch-variance effect. Averaged over the design's two temperatures, \(T = 1\) and \(10^{0.2}\), as for the 0.5B model, the excess over greedy decoding is 17.7 points ([9.3, 25.6]); at \(T = 10^{0.2}\) alone it is 44.8 points (53 against 10 of 96), and at \(T = 1\), where the soft pipeline answers none correctly and changed one answer, it is negative. The forced greedy baseline is a computational comparator, not a useful-answer baseline: it answers 1 of the 96 correctly. This short-budget effect does not need the float64 map's chaos. In float64, no answer of the 0.5B pipeline changed within the 32 steps; the bfloat16 discrepancies are consistent with rounding differences accumulating through continuous feedback. A discrete argmax absorbs differences smaller than its margin, but not over a long feedback run in a pipeline that answers poorly ([Soft Thinking as published](#soft-thinking-as-published), below). In the 7B model at \(T = 10^{0.2}\), where the float64 loop amplifies an injected perturbation (median \(+0.034\) nats per step), even the rounding-level difference between the float64 layouts changed 5% of the answers. An exploratory causal test supports this reading. Following a suggestion of an external review, it reran the 0.5B pipeline at \(T = 1\). It used 128 newly drawn additions, each run once alone as a reference and then in a batch of four. In the batch, two conditions start from the reference's prompt state, and the same decoder, run alone, reads off both of their answers. In the free condition the soft phase runs on its own. In the reset condition the target problem's cache (the attention keys and values that the model has stored for the tokens it has already read) and its logits are replaced by the reference's before every soft step. Each step then runs in the batch, but only one step at a time: the rounding difference that one step makes is not carried into the next. The test ran first on a workstation GPU, where the unmodified pipeline changed its answers with the layout in 74% of the problems, against 56% on the H100 of the test fixed in advance. In bfloat16 the answer changed in 88 of the 128 problems (69%) in the free condition and in 7 (5.5%) in the reset condition, a difference of 63 points (95% interval [55, 72]). Of the problems that changed in only one condition, 82 changed without the reset and 1 with it (exact McNemar test, a standard test for paired yes-or-no outcomes: \(p = 2\times10^{-23}\)). Accuracy stayed between 23 and 25% in every condition. One batched step moves the target's logits by a median 1.5% of their norm. In the free condition the median difference grows to 0.79 of that norm by step 32, while in the reset condition the median per step stays between 1.3 and 3.1%. In float32 the free condition's drift grows about 140-fold over the 32 steps but stays near \(10^{-4}\), and 3 of the 128 answers changed (none with the reset). The test replicates on an H100 and in Qwen2.5-7B. In bfloat16 on the H100 the answer changed in 60 of the 128 problems (47%) without the reset and in 1 (0.8%) with it in Qwen2.5-0.5B (at \(T = 1\)), and in 52 (41%) against none in Qwen2.5-7B (at \(T = 10^{0.2}\)), with exact McNemar \(p \le 5\times10^{-16}\). In the 7B model even the float32 answers changed, in 33 of the 128 problems (26%), against none with the reset. On the H100 most batched bfloat16 steps reproduce the reference bit for bit (the reset condition's median step distance is 0), and the free loop amplifies the rare step that does not. No condition's accuracy differed from the reference's by more than 5 points, although 128 problems per condition do not show that accuracy is unchanged. Within this budget, then, the batch layout changes low-precision answers because the loop carries each step's rounding forward and amplifies it, not because the last steps alone are fragile. These counts compare the extracted numbers, as the test fixed in advance does. Until 19 October 2026 the reset test compared the decoded answer texts instead, which also counts the same number followed by different text, and it reported higher counts (102 and 14 on the workstation; 85 and 2, and 82 and 2, on the H100). An earlier version of this note quoted those counts. Both the corrected and the original summaries are kept with the test's records. Two horizons thus matter. Within a short budget, continuous feedback in low precision makes answers depend on the batch, and where the loop expands, even float64 rounding does. Over longer runs, a chaotic regime amplifies float64 rounding into different readout tokens, on the schedule its Lyapunov exponent sets. ### Soft Thinking as published {#soft-thinking-as-published} The tests above used a short pipeline built for this study. A test whose design was fixed before any data, and amended once, also before any data, to run on an H100 GPU, ran Soft Thinking with its published settings on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct in bfloat16. The settings are concept tokens (the fed-back weighted averages of token embeddings) restricted to the 15 most probable tokens, \(T = 0.6\) and 64 soft steps. The test used 256 GSM8K training problems (GSM8K is a standard set of grade-school math word problems) that no earlier run had scored. Only the batch layout changed, between batches of 8 and of 16 prompts of equal length without padding, and the answer changed for 21.1% of the problems (54 of 256; 95% interval [16.3, 26.1], computed by resampling whole batches). This confirms the prediction of more than 10%. The batches departed from the design in one respect. Because a batch holds prompts of equal length, without padding, the test's harness filled each group of equal-length problems from one shared pool of filler prompts, and where that pool ran short, both layouts received the same batch. Rebuilding the batches from the tokenizer shows that 16 of the 256 problems ran in identical batches in both layouts; none of their answers changed, and among the other 240 problems the rate is 54 of 240 (22.5%). Some batches were also short, holding fewer prompts than their nominal size: 11 of the 78 batches of 8 and 26 of the 77 batches of 16. Each secondary prediction compares another setting with the published one on the same 256 problems (paired differences of the change rates, intervals clustered by batch, exact McNemar tests, a standard test for paired yes-or-no outcomes); each predicted a lower rate: - Replaying, in both layouts, the soft tokens recorded in a reference run, so that the fed-back tokens are identical: 5.9% (difference 15.2 points, [10.4, 20.2], \(p = 8\times10^{-9}\)). Lower, as predicted. - 16 soft steps instead of 64: 6.6% (difference 14.5 points, [10.0, 19.0], \(p = 4\times10^{-7}\)). Lower, as predicted. - Ordinary greedy chain-of-thought decoding: 2.3%, at 89% accuracy (difference 18.8 points, [13.7, 23.6], \(p = 10^{-11}\)). Lower, as predicted. - Feeding back only the most probable token: 17.6% (difference 3.5 points, [−2.9, 10.3], \(p = 0.35\)). The test cannot tell the two apart, so this prediction failed. The three confirmed differences would survive a correction for the four tests by a wide margin. The fourth is a difference that the test does not resolve: discrete feedback through the same pipeline changes nearly as many answers as continuous feedback does, although the interval does not establish that the two are equal. The full vocabulary gave 22.3% (no prediction). Most changes are between wrong answers: through the soft pipeline this model answers only 22 to 30% of the problems correctly, and the layout changes whether the answer is correct for 6.2% of the problems. In float64, small perturbations injected into the same pipeline mostly shrink over its observed runs: on 1312 and 1314 of the 1319 GSM8K test problems (full vocabulary and the 15 most probable tokens), a perturbation of \(10^{-10}\) ended below its initial size, and none changed an answer. These changes therefore do not require the float64 map's chaos: the feedback carries bfloat16 rounding differences forward until they change answers in a pipeline that answers only 22 to 30% of the problems correctly, and it does so for discrete feedback as well. ### How the dependence builds up {#dependence-builds-up} The test above read each answer once, after the full run of soft steps. A further exploratory study watched the dependence on the batch layout grow. It read the answers of the same pipeline after every doubling of the number of soft steps, from 2 to 128, so after 2, 4, 8 and so on up to 128 steps of feedback. It used 200 GSM8K test problems, two temperatures (0.6 and 1.2), and six steering strengths along the hostility direction (\(\alpha\) from \(-0.02\) to \(0.05\), where \(\alpha\) sets how strongly the hostility vector is added to the model's hidden state and \(\alpha = 0\) is the unsteered model). The two batch layouts agree on 90 to 96% of the answers after 2 steps and on 51 to 70% after 128, in every configuration. By the end of the run, many more answers depend on the layout than after the first steps. Among the problems whose layouts disagree, the median first disagreement comes after 8 steps. A batch-layout difference can change an answer in two different ways. Small perturbations of the float64 loop can shrink over the run, while the feedback still carries the rounding differences of bfloat16 forward until they change answers. Or the loop itself can be sensitive, so that small differences grow. Float64 copies of the same configurations, started \(10^{-10}\) apart, separate the two. In float64 the rounding error is far smaller than that offset, so an answer that changes between the copies shows that the loop itself amplifies small differences. - **Unsteered or weakly steered** (\(|\alpha| \le 0.02\)). The copies change the answer text of at most 1.5% of the problems. The answers are barely sensitive to these float64 perturbations, so the bfloat16 disagreements are consistent with rounding carried forward by the feedback. - **Strongly steered** (\(\alpha = 0.05\)). The copies change the answer text of 13.5% of the problems at \(T = 0.6\) and 27.5% at \(T = 1.2\), and the extracted number, the final answer itself, of 4.5 and 9.0%. The loop itself is then sensitive, but accuracy has fallen to between 0.5 and 2.5% in either layout. In this model, then, the regime in which Soft Thinking is useful is the regime of accumulated rounding, not of chaos. Where the loop's own sensitivity appears, the pipeline no longer solves the problems. ### Reasoning models that answer well {#reasoning-models} Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct answers few of these problems correctly through the soft pipeline, so most of its changed answers are changes between wrong answers. That leaves open whether the same thing happens to a model that solves the problems. A second test, also with its design fixed before any data, used reasoning models, as the Soft Thinking paper did. A reasoning model is a language model trained to work through a problem at length before it commits to an answer. It writes this working inside a thinking block, a stretch of text that opens with a special marker and closes with an end-of-thinking token; only what follows the block counts as the answer. Soft Thinking replaces the tokens of that block with concept tokens, so the thinking becomes a continuous feedback loop of the kind this note studies. The three models were DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B and QwQ-32B. - **Thinking.** Each prompt in a batch (a row) thinks in concept tokens (the 15 most probable tokens, \(T = 0.6\)) until its most probable next token is the one that ends the thinking block, or until 1536 steps, a cap on how long it may think. - **Answering.** It then answers by sampling ordinary discrete tokens, with the random numbers shared between the two layouts, so that the sampling itself makes the same draws in both and any difference comes from the arithmetic. - **Comparison.** The comparison branch thinks with discrete tokens sampled the same way, as ordinary reasoning models do. - **Layouts.** On GSM8K problems not used before, the batches held 8 or 16 prompts of equal length. On the problems of MATH-500 (a set of competition mathematics problems) whose answers are integers, each problem ran alone or as eight copies of itself. In the first run, the tokenizer of DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B, the component that turns text into tokens, loaded wrongly: it dropped the spaces and line breaks of every prompt. The model then thought far less and answered 45% of a check set correctly, against 83% with the correct tokenizer in bfloat16 and 81% in float64. Both of its combinations were rerun with the correct tokenizer, a change made after the data and disclosed as such. Over the five primary combinations of model and task, the batch layout changed 27.1% of the soft-thinking answers (243 of 896; 95% interval [24.7, 29.5]), confirming the prediction of more than 5%. This pooled rate is a weighted summary of these five combinations, which mix two tasks and two ways of changing the layout, not a general susceptibility of the models. The prediction holds in every version of the pooling, including the original run (29.6%) and the run without both combinations of this model (21.9%). - **All three models change their answers.** All three models changed their GSM8K answers with the layout alone: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B for 14.5% of the problems ([10.9, 18.0]) at 88 to 90% accuracy, QwQ-32B for 19.5% ([16.4, 22.3]) at 86 to 87%, and DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B for 28.9% ([23.4, 34.4]) at 74 to 77%. The two layouts disagreed on correctness for 11.7, 14.5 and 18.0% of the problems. - **Discrete thinking also changes many answers.** On GSM8K, discrete sampled thinking changed 10.2, 19.9 and 21.5% of the answers for the same three models. Only in DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B did soft thinking change more, by 7.4 points ([1.9, 12.9]; exact McNemar \(p = 0.029\), not corrected for the five combinations), and there it answered correctly 4.7 points less often ([−8.6, −0.8]; McNemar \(p = 0.096\)). The intervals resample whole batches, while the exact McNemar test treats the problems as independent pairs, so the two can disagree, as they do for this accuracy difference, whose interval excludes zero although its McNemar \(p\) is 0.096. Elsewhere no soft-minus-plain difference is significant, which does not show that the two are equal. In these pipelines the effect did not require continuous thinking: long sampled feedback in bfloat16 showed it too. - **Another GPU.** On an A100 instead of an H100, the first model's soft rate was 11.7% (difference 2.7 points, [−1.6, 6.6]), a separate replication on a second GPU type. The difference is not significant, which again does not establish that the two GPUs give equal rates. - **Where the budget bites.** Where the budget cut the reasoning short, accuracy was lower and the layout changed more answers. On MATH-500, where half or more of the problems reached the thinking cap, it changed 61% of the answers of DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B (44 to 48% correct) and 67% of those of DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B (39 to 42% correct). - **Nearly all of the changes come from long runs.** Over the three models, of the 161 GSM8K answers that the layout changed with soft thinking, 158 came from problems in which the thinking budget (1536 steps) or the answer budget (256 tokens) was reached in at least one layout, and so did all 132 changes with sampled thinking. Among problems that finished within both budgets in both layouts, the layout changed 3 of 480 soft answers and none of 477 sampled ones. **Cold Stop and a longer budget.** These runs did not use the Cold Stop rule of the Soft Thinking paper, which ends thinking once the entropy of the next-token distribution, a measure of how undecided the model is, has stayed below 0.01 nats for 256 steps. An exploratory rerun used it, with a thinking budget of 4096 steps instead of 1536. Cold Stop ended thinking in only 6 of the 512 soft rows and in none of the 512 sampled rows: the models nearly always ended their thinking themselves. The layout still changed the answers: - DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B on 128 GSM8K problems: 8.6% (soft) and 17.2% (sampled); - the same model on MATH-500: 50.0 and 54.7%; - QwQ-32B on 64 GSM8K problems: 17.2 and 9.4%. The soft-minus-sampled difference changes sign between these combinations, so neither kind of thinking is consistently more affected. On the same type of GPU, every row that ended thinking on its own within the original 1536 steps was reproduced exactly in its saved switch step and answer, so the changes come from the rows that the original budget cut short; the DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B GSM8K rerun ran on a different H100 variant. The rerun is therefore a modified configuration, not just a longer budget: it also added the Soft Thinking stopping rule and, for that model, ran on another H100 variant, so these results do not establish the rate for reasoning that completes. In the main runs, then, reasoning models that answer 86 to 90% of the GSM8K problems correctly changed 14.5 and 19.5% of their answers when only the batch around them changed, the two layouts disagreeing on correctness for 11.7 and 14.5% of the problems, and ordinary sampled reasoning with the same random numbers changed a similar share. Nearly all of these changes occurred on problems that reached the thinking or answer budget in at least one layout. The next test asks where these changes come from. **Whether this is chaos.** A batch-layout change can flip an answer in two ways ([How the dependence builds up](#dependence-builds-up)): the feedback can carry bfloat16 rounding forward until it changes an answer, even where small float64 perturbations shrink, or the loop itself can amplify small differences. To tell them apart, float64 copies of the same pipeline were run. Each copy's first soft token was displaced from the base row's by a relative \(10^{-10}\), far below any rounding difference of bfloat16, and every copy shared the base row's random numbers, so the only difference between a copy and its base row was that tiny displacement. The three models respond differently. - **DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B.** 216 of 256 copies ended the thinking at a distance from their base row below the initial displacement, and 2.3% changed the answer. This is consistent with its layout changes arising mainly from bfloat16 rounding carried through the feedback, as in Qwen2.5-7B; it does not show that the loop contracts everywhere. - **QwQ-32B and DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B.** More than half of the copies ended above the initial displacement (131 of 192 and 145 of 256). Fitted only over the steps where the distance lay between ten times the displacement and \(10^{-3}\), the median growth rates were 0.011 and 0.008 per step: slow growth. The displacement alone changed 13.5 and 18.4% of the answers, respectively. In those two models, then, the loop's own sensitivity contributes to the answer changes: the thinking loop itself slowly amplifies tiny differences. It is a weak, finite-time instability over about a thousand thinking steps, and it acts on top of the rounding rather than replacing it. Three cautions apply. This is not an asymptotic chaos measurement, which would need far longer runs than a thinking block lasts. Some copies ended their thinking before their base row did (14 in DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B, 23 in QwQ-32B). And the copies of one problem are not independent of each other. The test used 128 problems for each of the two smaller models and 96 for QwQ-32B. **Does a loop that is not chaotic protect against batching differences?** Only when the rounding starts tiny. ### What the regime does not predict {#what-the-regime-does-not-predict} A test fixed in advance asked whether a chaotic loop marks worse answers in ordinary decoding. It labeled 4000 newly drawn products of two two-digit numbers by the regime of the unsteered Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct's own loop at \(\log_{10}T = 0.40\). Prompts with a chaotic loop are answered less accurately by ordinary sampling, by 7.1 points (95% interval [4.8, 9.3]), but the gap vanishes once seven difficulty covariates, fixed before sampling, enter the fit: the label's coefficient is +0.15 points ([−1.4, 1.7], permutation \(p = 0.84\)). In a post hoc fit, the entropy of the first answer token alone absorbs nearly all of the gap. That fits the measurements above: the loop's chaotic cells have more competing next tokens than its periodic ones, and a model unsure of its first token also answers worse. Within a prompt no association is detected either. The first 1000 of these prompts were also steered slightly, at block 14, along philosophy, hostility-versus-kindness and a random direction. The strength, 1% of the norm of the residual stream, is the largest at which greedy accuracy stayed within 5 points of the unsteered model on the first 200 of these prompts, so the calibration overlaps the test prompts; on the 1000 prompts greedy accuracy is 0.87 to 0.89 under the pushes, against 0.89 unsteered. Even these slight pushes change the loop's label between conditions for 508 of the 1000 prompts. An analysis fixed before the data compared the conditions within each prompt, giving every prompt and every condition its own baseline (fixed effects, over 3992 prompt-condition rows). In it, a chaotic label is associated with a change of +0.36 points in the accuracy of the prompt's ordinary sampled answers (95% interval [−0.36, 1.08]; permutation test within prompts, \(p = 0.34\)). That is an association, not a causal effect of entering chaos: the pushes can act on the answers through other paths as well. Accuracy does not peak at the edge of chaos either. Deeply periodic, edge (\(\lvert\lambda\rvert \le 0.1\)) and deeply chaotic prompts are answered alike, with all three adjusted contrasts within [−3.1, 3.0] points. These are nulls at this precision; they do not show that the regime has no effect. ### Sensitivity without control {#sensitivity-without-control} If differences far below rounding can change what a soft-thinking loop answers, can someone choose which answer it gives? The two are different risks. A loop that is merely sensitive is unreliable: its answer can change for no visible reason. A loop whose sensitivity can be aimed would be open to attack: a small, deliberate change to one hidden vector could make it give a chosen wrong answer, and nothing in the visible text would show it. In the one setting tested here, the answer is mostly no. Small perturbations of a fed-back token change many answers, but even an optimized perturbation rarely moves the answer to the value it was optimized for. **The test.** An exploratory test used the soft-thinking pipeline of Qwen2.5-0.5B on two-digit additions, in float32, with 16 soft steps, at temperatures 0.3 and 1.0. The settings were chosen on 16 development problems, and the test used 64 other problems. For each problem the attack aimed at one fixed wrong answer, the correct sum plus or minus 10, and could change only the first soft token. The perturbation added to it was confined to one token norm: it could be at most as long as that token itself. It came from 20 steps of gradient ascent on the log-probability of the target answer, each followed by a projection back into that radius (projected gradient ascent). As a baseline, random search tried 45 random directions of that length and kept the best, with at least as much computation. To count as control, the optimizer had to reach the target at least 10 points more often than random search. **What happened.** Only problem-temperature pairs that the unperturbed pipeline answered correctly count, 101 of the 128, because the attack tries to turn a correct answer into a chosen wrong one. On the 64 test problems, the optimized perturbation reached the target in 5 of 101 problem-temperature pairs, and random search in none: a difference of 4.2 points with each problem weighted equally (95% interval [0.8, 8.3]), below the advantage of 10 points that the design required. Yet perturbations of that size do move the answer. A single random direction changed it in about a third of the pairs (one random direction: 34 of the 101 eligible pairs), almost never to the target. The loop is sensitive, then, but its sensitivity does not point anywhere in particular: the answer changes, just not to the value the attacker chose. **Where aiming is easier.** The same optimization applied to the last soft token before the answer cue, the text that prompts the answer, reached the target in 14 of the 101. A change to the first soft token has to pass through all 16 steps of the loop before the answer is read; a change to the last one does not. In this pipeline, then, the loop gives an attacker less leverage early than late. **What the test does not show.** It does not show that chaotic loops resist steering. The tested temperatures are ones at which the loop contracts for most problems (on the development problems, 10% and 38% of twins expanded, that is, drifted away from their loop instead of back toward it, with median growth rates of −0.131 and −0.058 per step), where the pipeline still answers correctly. The perturbation sizes and the optimizer were chosen on the development problems, and the test covers one small model, one task and one perturbation size. ### Taming and using the sensitivity {#taming-sensitivity} If the loop's sensitivity is what makes answers depend on the batch, two practical questions follow: whether the theory points to a remedy, and whether the sensitivity can be put to use. Two exploratory tests asked them with Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct in bfloat16, on 512 unused GSM8K training problems, 16 at each of 32 prompt lengths, fixed before any outcome, with soft thinking over the 15 most probable tokens at \(T = 0.6\) for 64 steps. **A remedy from the theory: capping the readout gain.** The derivative of one step factorizes into a network factor and a readout factor ([Why the loop can be chaotic](#why-the-loop-can-be-chaotic)), and along recorded orbits of the 0.5B model the growth that steering adds comes mainly from the readout: the softmax at temperature \(T\) amplifies small changes most when several tokens compete and the temperature is low. The readout gain measures that amplification. The remedy follows directly: at each step, lower the temperature until a proxy of the readout gain falls below a cap, so that no step can amplify much (the cap could not be met on about 1% of steps, at exact ties). With such a cap, the share of answers that the batch layout changed fell from 27.7 to about 23% (by 4.1 to 4.7 points at three caps), and accuracy did not fall. **The control that matters: a uniform temperature.** Capping the gain works by lowering the temperature where needed, so part of its effect could come from a lower temperature as such, wherever it is applied. A control that simply ran at \(T = 0.5\) at every step separates the two. It was added after the first result was seen, so it is itself an exploratory check. It gained as much accuracy, and the caps' extra reduction of changed answers relative to it (2.7 to 3.3 points) was not significant. The remedy is therefore modest, and it is not shown to work through the readout specifically rather than through a lower temperature overall. **Using the sensitivity: a vote over perturbed runs.** Self-consistency is a standard way to make a model more accurate: sample several answers to the same problem and keep the one given most often, a plurality vote. Since tiny perturbations already change soft-thinking answers, the perturbations themselves could supply the variety for such a vote. Eight runs, each with its first soft token displaced by a relative \(10^{-3}\), voted on each answer, the most frequent answer winning (a plurality vote). The vote showed no detectable accuracy gain over a single run (+0.2 points, [−1.0, 1.4]), although one displacement changed 20.2% of the answers on average. Ordinary sampled self-consistency with eight samples, by contrast, gained 5.6 points ([3.5, 8.1]). The perturbed runs differ, but rarely toward the correct answer, and the problems whose perturbed runs disagreed were also the ones answered correctly least often: the sensitivity marks hard problems rather than offering a route to their answers. ### Weight quantization and the attractors {#weight-quantization} Deployed models are often quantized: their weights are stored with fewer bits. Quantization is usually checked one step at a time, by how close the quantized model's next-token distributions stay to the original's. An exploratory test asked whether that check certifies the closed loop. Every linear weight of the decoder blocks of Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct was quantized, either in 8-bit blocks (as in the `Q8_0` format of llama.cpp) or in symmetric 4-bit blocks, while the arithmetic stayed in float64. The unsteered loop then ran on 48 prompts not used in development, at 8 temperatures over \(\log_{10}T \in [-0.5, 0.5]\), from 2 starts each. A fixed random logit bias, scaled so that its one-step divergence matches the 8-bit variant's, served as an unstructured control: noise of the same one-step size, with no structure from the weights. - **8-bit.** The one-step distributions stay close. On the original model's attractor states, the mean Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence, a standard measure of how far one probability distribution lies from another, is 0.0028 nats, and the most probable token agrees in 94.5% of states. The share of starts that end on a periodic orbit of period at most 8 shows no detectable change (+1.2 points, 95% interval [−1.9, 4.2]). Yet 14.1% of the starts end in a different class (periodic, chaotic or neither) or with a different period, as do 15.0% under the random bias of the same one-step size. These changes concentrate at the temperatures where the attractors change. - **4-bit.** The share rises by 6.8 points ([2.6, 11.0]), mostly because the edge of a chaotic band turns periodic. Its one-step distributions, however, are far from the original's: the mean divergence is 0.83 nats, and the most probable token agrees in only 52% of states. In this model, then, a close one-step check was consistent with unchanged statistics of the closed loop but did not fix the attractor that an individual run reaches. No effect of quantization was found beyond that of unstructured noise of the same one-step size. ### Chaos onset and repetition in sampled text {#onset-repetition} As temperature rises, a prompt's soft-token loop turns chaotic at some point, its chaos onset. Ordinary sampled text changes with temperature too: at low temperature it often falls into repeating a phrase verbatim, and at higher temperature it stops. An exploratory test asked whether the first temperature predicts the second, which would make the loop's dynamics a guide to a familiar failure of ordinary generation. The test used Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct on 24 prompts reserved for it, and it did not detect the proposed positive association. The Spearman correlation, which compares the rank order of the two temperatures across prompts, is −0.23 (95% interval [−0.60, 0.25], permutation \(p = 0.28\)). The interval includes zero, so the test cannot tell this from no relation at all; that is not the same as evidence of no association, and the interval is wide. One sensitivity analysis (counting orbits of period up to 32 as periodic, and clustering by system prompt) even gives an interval that excludes zero on the negative side, [−0.62, −0.18], the opposite of the proposed direction. At matched temperature, the repetition rates of chaotic and periodic cells differed by 0.003 (interval [−0.013, 0.023]), but both regimes were present at only 8 of the 24 temperatures, so this comparison rests on few points. In 13 of the 15 prompts where both onsets were observed, sampled text stopped repeating below the loop's chaos onset. The median gap over these 15 is 0.42 decades of temperature (a decade is a tenfold change in \(T\)). This is a null result in the narrow sense: the test did not detect the effect it was designed to find. The soft-token loop and sampled decoding with a growing context are different systems, and this test did not find a bridge between them. ### Coupled agents (a behavioral check) {#coupled-agents} Two Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct agents solving the same multiplication problem each fed back a mixture of thoughts: a fraction \(1 - c\) of their own concept token and a fraction \(c\) of the other agent's, the coupling, while their contexts grew (64 problems, 8 pairs each; float32; exploratory). At \(c = 0.25\), agreement on the same wrong answer rose by only 1.6 points ([−0.6, 3.9]), and accuracy fell by 5.5 points, as it did when each agent instead received messages replayed from another pair's run. At \(c = 0.5\), mixing gives the two agents equal next inputs, although their growing contexts differ. They then agreed on 96% of answers, including 41.0% of pairs that gave the same wrong number, and accuracy was 12.5 points lower than for independent agents. That suggests that the history of a steering schedule can matter, not only its present value. A system whose response depends on the path it took, and not only on its current settings, shows hysteresis; a magnet that stays magnetized after the field is removed is the textbook case. Two tests, a first exploratory one and then a confirmatory one, asked whether steering history matters for a decision with right and wrong answers. The model was Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct, thinking in soft tokens. It judged synthetic access-control requests against a supplied permission table, answering ALLOW or DENY, so every request had a correct answer. A permissive-versus-restrictive direction steered it at layer 18: a vector added to the model's hidden state that pushes it toward granting or toward refusing. Every run ended with 32 steps at the same steering strength (\(\alpha = 0.025\)). A confirmatory test guards against both. This pipeline appends what it writes to its context, which grows with every step, unlike the fixed-size state of the soft-token map studied in most of this note. What the loop wrote during the excursion stays in that growing context, so a memory of the context is the plausible mechanism, although these tests do not isolate it. This is history dependence of the protocol, not a demonstration of hysteresis in a fixed-size state. One model and one schedule were tested, in float32, with two wordings of one direction. ### Whether the hidden state changes answers {#hidden-state-answers} In band chaos the loop writes an exactly repeating text while its state moves chaotically: the same token wins at each position, while the probabilities behind it keep changing ([Chaos behind a repeating text](#chaos-behind-a-repeating-text)). ### The fold and its ghost {#the-fold-and-its-ghost} At \(\log_{10}T = -0.115\) the 2-cycle `" is it"` dies in a fold at \(\alpha_c = 0.06279827\): its float64 multiplier equals 1 to within \(3\times10^{-13}\), and the next has modulus 0.037. There it meets an unstable 2-cycle, and both vanish (Figure 26a, b). Near a fold, center-manifold reduction restricts the local dynamics to the critical direction, however many other dimensions there are, as long as the other multipliers stay off the unit circle. In the critical coordinate \(u\) of the second iterate \(G = F^2\) (two steps of the loop, one turn of the 2-cycle), the fold's normal form is \[ u' = u + a\varepsilon + bu^2, \qquad \varepsilon = \alpha - \alpha_c . \] Read it as a recipe for one turn: the coordinate \(u\) moves by a constant push \(a\varepsilon\), set by the distance from the fold, plus a term \(bu^2\) that grows away from the fold point. Below the fold (\(a\varepsilon\) and \(b\) of opposite sign) the two terms can cancel, and the two cancellation points are the attracting 2-cycle and its unstable partner. Beyond the fold they cannot cancel, and \(u\) drifts, slowly where \(u\) is small. Both coefficients come from the network's own derivatives: \(a = -4.834\) per unit \(\alpha\) and \(b = -25.4285\), so \(ab = 122.93\). **Where the two coefficients come from, and what the formula leaves out.** Let \(q\) be the critical direction, the eigenvector of the derivative \(DG\) whose multiplier is \(+1\), scaled to unit length, and let \(\ell\) be the matching left eigenvector, scaled so that \(\ell^{\top}q = 1\); the coordinate \(u\) measures position along \(q\). Then \[ a = \ell^{\top}\,\frac{\partial G}{\partial\alpha}, \qquad b = \tfrac12\,\ell^{\top}D^2G[q, q] : \] \(a\) is how strongly a change of the steering strength pushes the state along the critical direction, and \(b\) is the curvature of the two-step map along it, the second derivative read off in that direction ([Kuznetsov and Meijer, 2019](#ref-kuznetsov-2019)). The normal form is the quadratic truncation of \(G\) on its center manifold: it keeps the lowest-order terms and drops those of order \(u^3\), \(\varepsilon u\) and \(\varepsilon^2\). It applies because three conditions hold here: the multiplier \(+1\) is simple (no other multiplier sits at \(+1\)), \(a\) and \(b\) are both nonzero, and every other multiplier lies inside the unit circle ([Kuznetsov, 2023](#ref-kuznetsov-2023)). A multiplier at \(+1\) does not by itself mean a fold. In a map with a symmetry, or with an orbit that is forced to persist on both sides of the parameter value, the push \(a\) vanishes, and a multiplier \(+1\) then marks a pitchfork, where one orbit splits into three, or a transcritical bifurcation, where two orbits cross and exchange their stability. No symmetry of the soft-token map forces a pitchfork and no persistent branch forces a transcritical exchange, so these conditions make the point a fold. **Two checks of the coefficients.** The stable branch gives an independent estimate: extrapolating its multipliers through \((1 - \mu)^2 / (4(\alpha_c - \alpha)) \to ab\) yields 123.1 with a quadratic fit (120.6 with a linear one). An independent implementation of the forward map and solver recovers \(\alpha_c\) to \(6\times10^{-15}\) and \(a\) to \(3\times10^{-12}\). Its \(b\), from nested automatic differentiation, is \(-25.42846\); ours differs from it by about \(2.2\times10^{-6}\) relatively, the finite-step bias of our difference table. The resulting \(ab = 122.927\) leaves every passage prediction below unchanged. **The ghost.** Beyond the fold the 2-cycle is gone, but its ghost slows the dynamics: trajectories crawl through a narrow channel where the orbit used to be, like a ball rolling over a nearly flat saddle of a landscape. We started trajectories at the beginning of the channel (\(v = -U\), in the oriented coordinate \(v = \mathrm{sign}(b)\,u\), with \(U = 0.1/\lvert b\rvert\)) or at its midpoint (\(v = 0\)) and counted iterates of \(G\) until \(v > U\). At four distances from the fold, the measured counts match the iterated normal form within one iterate, with no fitted parameter (Table 5 and Figure 27), and a displacement of the start of the same size, along one random direction that leaves \(u\) unchanged (the transverse kick of Table 5), changes the count by at most one; other directions and sizes were not tested. **The passage in closed form.** Treated as a smooth flow rather than a sequence of steps, the normal form gives the number of iterates from a start \(v_{\mathrm{in}}\) to the exit \(U\) in closed form, \[ n(v_{\mathrm{in}}) = \frac{1}{\kappa}\left[\arctan\frac{\lvert b\rvert U}{\kappa} - \arctan\frac{\lvert b\rvert v_{\mathrm{in}}}{\kappa}\right], \qquad \kappa = \sqrt{ab\,\varepsilon} . \] The arctangent levels off far from the bottleneck, so a full passage, from \(-U\) to \(U\), approaches \(\pi/\kappa\) only when the channel is much wider than the bottleneck itself, \(U \gg \sqrt{\lvert a\rvert\varepsilon/\lvert b\rvert}\). The counts in Table 5 come from iterating the quadratic map step by step instead; the two forms of the forecast are compared in [Passage times predicted in advance](#passage-times-predicted-in-advance). Left to itself, a trajectory near the fold alternates between laminar phases in the bottleneck (40 to 70 iterates each) and bursts away from it (Figure 26d). In a laminar phase it crawls through the bottleneck close to where the 2-cycle was and moves almost periodically; a burst is a short excursion out of the channel, after which the trajectory is reinjected into it. This alternation is type-I intermittency ([Pomeau and Manneville, 1980](#ref-pomeau-1980)), whose laminar phases lengthen as \(\varepsilon^{-1/2}\) toward the fold ([Hirsch, Huberman, and Scalapino, 1982](#ref-hirsch-1982)). Laminar is the fluid-dynamics term for the smooth stretches of a flow between turbulent bursts. The diagram below draws the bottleneck that these passages cross, from the normal form itself.
